article.title: Why Peak Performance Is Not the Same as Sustainable Capacity
article.summary: Sustainable capacity is the repeatable load a runtime can carry without continuously damaging recovery, interfaces, or future capability—not the maximum load it once pushed through.

blocks.text: Sustainable capacity is the repeatable load a runtime can carry without continuously damaging recovery, interfaces, or future capability—not the maximum load it once pushed through.

Capacity is often judged by remembered peaks. A person once worked at extreme intensity, a team once ran several major projects at the same time, or a system once handled a very high load. These records prove that short-term mobilization happened; they do not prove that the same intensity can be repeated indefinitely.

Book III separates short-term capability from maintenance capacity. Short-term capability asks what can be pushed through under special conditions. Maintenance capacity asks how long the operation can be repeated without continuously degrading recovery, interfaces, and future capability. Recovery time, reserve, and structural friction therefore belong inside the calculation.

Short bursts often borrow from the future. More attention today may require more recovery later; concentrating people on one project delays other work; bypassing steps in an artificial system can create later validation and correction costs. Exceeding normal capacity is not automatically wrong, but the runtime must know that it is using reserve and know how that reserve will be restored.

Reserve is not waste. When time, people, money, attention, and technical paths are kept permanently full, every surprise immediately displaces something else. Resilient structures keep some response space unused so that change can be absorbed without instantly damaging another area.

Capacity also depends on interfaces. A runtime can possess many resources and still be unable to use them effectively because responsibility is unclear, approvals are concentrated, or information is difficult to translate. Capacity management therefore asks not only “how much do we have?” but “how much can this structure use repeatedly and reliably?”

blocks.label: Key judgment
blocks.text: Long-term capacity must include recovery time and reserve.

blocks.label: Reality Question
blocks.text: Are you planning around repeatable capacity, or treating one historical peak as a permanent baseline?
